lessons.name: What is Observability — definition, pillars, and why it matters
lessons.desc: Observability is the ability to measure the internal state of a system by examining its outputs (logs, metrics, traces). It answers "what is happening?" without deploying new code. Originated from control theory: a syste
lessons.what:
Observability is the ability to measure the internal state of a system by examining its outputs (logs, metrics, traces). It answers "what is happening?" without deploying new code.
  • Originated from control theory: a system is observable if you can infer internal state from external outputs
  • Three pillars: logs (discrete events), metrics (aggregated data), traces (request lifecycle)
  • Observability != monitoring — monitoring tells you something is wrong, observability tells you WHY
  • Enables debugging of unknown-unknowns: failures you didn't anticipate or define alert rules for
  • Key metric: MTTD (Mean Time to Detect) vs MTTR (Mean Time to Resolve) — observability reduces both
  • High-cardinality data (user IDs, request IDs) is essential for effective observability
lessons.why: Observability separates reactive firefighting from proactive system understanding — it's the foundation of running distributed systems in production.

lessons.name: Observability vs Monitoring — black box vs white box
lessons.desc: Monitoring watches known failure modes with predefined dashboards and alerts. Observability enables ad-hoc investigation of any system behavior. Monitoring: black box — observe system from outside, check predefined healt
lessons.what:
Monitoring watches known failure modes with predefined dashboards and alerts. Observability enables ad-hoc investigation of any system behavior.
  • Monitoring: black box — observe system from outside, check predefined health indicators
  • Observability: white box — instrument the system to expose internal state for exploration
  • Monitoring answers "is it working?" — observability answers "why isn't it working?"
  • Monitoring creates known-knowns — observability surfaces unknown-unknowns
  • Production: both are needed — monitoring for alerting, observability for root cause analysis
  • Shift: move from "what can we monitor?" to "what questions will we need to answer?"
lessons.why: The distinction determines your entire operations strategy — monitoring-only leaves you blind to novel failures.

lessons.name: Cardinality & Dimensionality — low vs high
lessons.desc: Cardinality refers to the number of unique values a label/tag dimension can have. Low cardinality: HTTP methods (GET/POST). High cardinality: user IDs, request IDs. Low cardinality ( Medium cardinality ( High cardinality
lessons.what:
Cardinality refers to the number of unique values a label/tag dimension can have. Low cardinality: HTTP methods (GET/POST). High cardinality: user IDs, request IDs.
  • Low cardinality (<100 values): HTTP status codes, deployment versions, availability zones
  • Medium cardinality (<10K values): service names, endpoint paths, error codes
  • High cardinality (millions): user IDs, session IDs, request IDs, IP addresses
  • Metrics engines (Prometheus) struggle with high cardinality — cardinality explosion kills performance
  • Tracing naturally handles high cardinality via span IDs and trace IDs
  • Strategy: use metrics for low-cardinality aggregations, traces for high-cardinality investigations
lessons.why: Cardinality is the #1 performance bottleneck in observability — choosing wrong dimensions makes systems slower or too expensive.

lessons.name: Maturity Model — levels of observability adoption
lessons.desc: Observability maturity model: level 0 (no instrumentation) → level 1 (basic metrics) → level 2 (pillars implemented) → level 3 (correlated telemetry) → level 4 (self-service, AI-assisted). Level 0 — Dark: no instrumentat
lessons.what:
Observability maturity model: level 0 (no instrumentation) → level 1 (basic metrics) → level 2 (pillars implemented) → level 3 (correlated telemetry) → level 4 (self-service, AI-assisted).
  • Level 0 — Dark: no instrumentation, SSH into servers, console.log debugging
  • Level 1 — Basic: infrastructure metrics (CPU/memory/disk), simple uptime monitoring
  • Level 2 — Instrumented: structured logging, RED metrics, basic tracing on critical paths
  • Level 3 — Correlated: OpenTelemetry, trace-log-metric correlation, SLO-based alerting
  • Level 4 — Proactive: AI-driven anomaly detection, auto-remediation, self-service observability platform
  • Most orgs sit at Level 2 — reaching Level 3 is the architect-level differentiator
lessons.why: Maturity models help you prioritize investments and communicate progress to stakeholders — know where you stand.

lessons.name: The Three Pillars deep dive: logs, metrics, traces
lessons.desc: Each pillar serves a different purpose: logs tell a story (what happened), metrics show trends (how many), traces map causality (where in the request flow). Logs: high verbosity, structured JSON, contain detailed context
lessons.what:
Each pillar serves a different purpose: logs tell a story (what happened), metrics show trends (how many), traces map causality (where in the request flow).
  • Logs: high verbosity, structured JSON, contain detailed context — expensive to store and query at scale
  • Metrics: lightweight, numeric, aggregated over time windows — lose individual request detail
  • Traces: capture request flow across services — provide causality but have sampling overhead
  • The pillars are not mutually exclusive — correlation between them is the real power
  • OpenTelemetry unifies all three: traces carry context, metrics aggregate, logs attach to spans
  • Analogy: logs = witness testimony, metrics = security camera summary, traces = surveillance footage
lessons.why: Understanding when to use each pillar (and their limitations) is the core skill of observability — no single pillar suffices.

lessons.name: Structured vs Unstructured Logging
lessons.desc: Structured logging emits machine-parseable records (JSON) with consistent fields. Unstructured logging emits free-text strings that require regex to extract meaning. Structured: {"level":"error","msg":"request failed","s
lessons.what:
Structured logging emits machine-parseable records (JSON) with consistent fields. Unstructured logging emits free-text strings that require regex to extract meaning.
  • Structured: {"level":"error","msg":"request failed","status":503,"duration_ms":4500,"trace_id":"abc123"}
  • Unstructured: "ERROR: request failed - took 4500ms" — needs regex to parse, fragile to format changes
  • JSON is the standard format — supports nested objects, arrays, and mixed types
  • Pino: fastest Node.js logger (~5x faster than Winston) with native JSON support
  • Logs should have: timestamp, level, message, service, trace_id, span_id, and domain-specific fields
  • Avoid logging PII, secrets, or large payloads — use log redaction and sampling
lessons.why: Structured logging is the baseline for any serious production system — unstructured logs are nearly impossible to query at scale.

lessons.name: Log Levels & Best Practices
lessons.desc: Log levels (fatal/error/warn/info/debug/trace) indicate severity. Production typically runs at info level, debug enabled per-request via feature flags. FATAL: application cannot continue — crash imminent, triggers on-cal
lessons.what:
Log levels (fatal/error/warn/info/debug/trace) indicate severity. Production typically runs at info level, debug enabled per-request via feature flags.
  • FATAL: application cannot continue — crash imminent, triggers on-call immediately
  • ERROR: request failed, operation degraded — needs investigation but app survives
  • WARN: unusual but handled — retry succeeded, fallback used, rate limit approaching
  • INFO: significant lifecycle events — deployment, config change, user signup
  • DEBUG: detailed context for troubleshooting — enable temporarily per-service via config
  • TRACE: function-level entry/exit — rarely used, high volume, typically only in dev
lessons.why: Correct log levels ensure signal-to-noise ratio in production — too verbose buries real issues, too sparse prevents debugging.

lessons.name: Centralized Logging — ELK Stack, Loki, and Log Shipping
lessons.desc: Centralized logging aggregates logs from all services into a searchable store. ELK (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) and Grafana Loki are the dominant stacks. ELK stack: Logstash parses/ships → Elasticsearch indexes → Ki
lessons.what:
Centralized logging aggregates logs from all services into a searchable store. ELK (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) and Grafana Loki are the dominant stacks.
  • ELK stack: Logstash parses/ships → Elasticsearch indexes → Kibana visualizes
  • Grafana Loki: push-based, stores compressed logs, indexes by labels (not full-text)
  • Log shipping agents: Filebeat (ELK), Promtail (Loki), Fluentd/Fluent Bit (vendor-neutral)
  • Logstash is heavy — Fluent Bit is preferred for edge/agent-side log collection
  • Loki is cheaper for high-volume logs (no full-text indexing) but limited query capabilities
  • Hot/warm/cold tiering: recent logs in fast storage (SSD), older in object storage (S3/GCS)
lessons.why: Logs on individual servers are useless in distributed systems — centralized search and correlation is mandatory.

lessons.name: Log Correlation & Aggregation — correlation IDs across services
lessons.desc: Correlation IDs (trace IDs) propagate across service boundaries to stitch together logs from a single request. Each service logs the same trace_id. Generate correlation ID at ingress (API gateway or load balancer) Propag
lessons.what:
Correlation IDs (trace IDs) propagate across service boundaries to stitch together logs from a single request. Each service logs the same trace_id.
  • Generate correlation ID at ingress (API gateway or load balancer)
  • Propagate via HTTP headers: x-request-id, x-correlation-id, or traceparent (W3C)
  • Each service extracts the ID and includes it in all log statements
  • AsyncLocalStorage (Node.js) scopes correlation ID per request across async boundaries
  • Aggregation: query "trace_id=abc123" across all services → single timeline view
  • Tools: Elastic APM, Grafana Tempo, Datadog trace-log correlation
lessons.why: Without correlation IDs, debugging a multi-service request requires manual log spelunking across disparate sources — it's the #1 productivity booster.

lessons.name: Log Sampling, Retention & Volume Management
lessons.desc: Log volume grows with traffic. Retention policies define how long logs live. Sampling reduces volume while preserving signal. Dynamic sampling: increase sampling rate during errors, decrease during normal operation Error
lessons.what:
Log volume grows with traffic. Retention policies define how long logs live. Sampling reduces volume while preserving signal.
  • Dynamic sampling: increase sampling rate during errors, decrease during normal operation
  • Error sampling: ALWAYS capture 100% of errors — sample only successful requests (1:10, 1:100)
  • Retention: hot (7 days, fast), warm (30 days, moderate), cold (1 year, cheap object store)
  • Log rotation: size-based (e.g., 100MB per file) or time-based (e.g., daily) with compression
  • Log lifecycle: stream → parse → enrich → index → store hot → tier warm → archive cold → delete
  • Rule of thumb: ~1-2 GB per million requests for structured JSON logs
lessons.why: Raw log volume grows linearly with traffic — without sampling and retention, storage costs explode beyond value.

lessons.name: Metric Types — Counter, Gauge, Histogram, Summary
lessons.desc: Counter (monotonically increasing), Gauge (up/down), Histogram (distribution of values), Summary (pre-computed quantiles). Each serves a different analytical purpose. Counter: only increases or resets to 0 — request coun
lessons.what:
Counter (monotonically increasing), Gauge (up/down), Histogram (distribution of values), Summary (pre-computed quantiles). Each serves a different analytical purpose.
  • Counter: only increases or resets to 0 — request count, errors, bytes sent. Use rate() to derive per-second
  • Gauge: goes up and down — memory usage, active connections, queue depth
  • Histogram: bucket-based distribution of observed values — request latency, response size
  • Histogram provides: count, sum, bucket counts — derive p50/p95/p99 via histogram_quantile()
  • Summary: pre-computed quantiles on the client side — less flexible but more accurate
  • Prometheus best practice: use Histogram over Summary — server-side quantile calculation is more flexible
lessons.why: Choosing the wrong metric type leads to incorrect analysis — counters vs gauges is a classic interview distinction.

lessons.name: RED Method vs USE Method
lessons.desc: RED: Rate, Errors, Duration (per service). USE: Utilization, Saturation, Errors (per resource). RED for services, USE for infrastructure. RED Method (Tom Wilkie): Rate (requests/sec), Errors (failed requests/sec), Durati
lessons.what:
RED: Rate, Errors, Duration (per service). USE: Utilization, Saturation, Errors (per resource). RED for services, USE for infrastructure.
  • RED Method (Tom Wilkie): Rate (requests/sec), Errors (failed requests/sec), Duration (latency distribution)
  • USE Method (Brendan Gregg): Utilization (% busy), Saturation (queue/demand), Errors (failure count)
  • RED applies to: microservices, APIs, databases, caches, message queues (as services)
  • USE applies to: CPU, memory, disk, network, GPU (as infrastructure resources)
  • RED + USE together give complete coverage — every service should have RED, every resource USE
  • Common RED dashboards: request rate graph, error ratio graph, latency heatmap (p50/p95/p99)
lessons.why: RED and USE are universal mental models for what to measure — they prevent blind spots in your monitoring strategy.

lessons.name: Prometheus & Grafana — pull model, metric collection, querying
lessons.desc: Prometheus scrapes metrics from instrumented targets via HTTP pull model. Grafana visualizes Prometheus data with dashboards. Prometheus: pull-based — scrapes /metrics endpoints at configurable intervals (default 15s) Se
lessons.what:
Prometheus scrapes metrics from instrumented targets via HTTP pull model. Grafana visualizes Prometheus data with dashboards.
  • Prometheus: pull-based — scrapes /metrics endpoints at configurable intervals (default 15s)
  • Service discovery: Kubernetes, Consul, DNS SRV, or static targets file
  • PromQL: rate(requests_total[5m]) per-second rate, histogram_quantile(0.99, ...) for p99
  • Grafana: dashboard as code via JSON — variables, templating, annotations, alerts
  • Recording rules: pre-compute expensive PromQL queries every 30s for dashboard performance
  • Alerting rules: evaluate in Prometheus and send to Alertmanager for routing/de-duplication
lessons.why: Prometheus + Grafana is the industry standard — knowing PromQL and dashboard design is expected at the architect level.

lessons.name: Service Level Metrics — SLI, SLO, SLA, Error Budgets
lessons.desc: SLI (Service Level Indicator): a raw measurement. SLO (Objective): target for SLI. SLA (Agreement): contractual commitment. Error budget: allowed failures = 100% - SLO. SLI examples: request latency p99, error ratio, ava
lessons.what:
SLI (Service Level Indicator): a raw measurement. SLO (Objective): target for SLI. SLA (Agreement): contractual commitment. Error budget: allowed failures = 100% - SLO.
  • SLI examples: request latency p99, error ratio, availability %, throughput
  • SLO: "99.9% of requests complete in <200ms over a 30-day rolling window"
  • Error budget = 100% - SLO — if SLO is 99.9%, error budget is 0.1% (43 min/month)
  • Burn rate: how fast you consume error budget — >1 burn rate means you will miss SLO
  • Multi-window burn rate alerts: detect fast burns (5m window) and slow burns (1h window)
  • SLA is business/legal — SLO is engineering — never set SLA tighter than internal SLO
lessons.why: SLOs drive engineering prioritization — error budgets tell you when to ship features vs fix reliability. Google SRE core concept.

lessons.name: Four Golden Signals — Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation
lessons.desc: Google SRE's four universal signals: Latency (time to serve), Traffic (demand volume), Errors (failure rate), Saturation (how full the service is). Latency: distinguish between success and error latency — slow errors mas
lessons.what:
Google SRE's four universal signals: Latency (time to serve), Traffic (demand volume), Errors (failure rate), Saturation (how full the service is).
  • Latency: distinguish between success and error latency — slow errors mask fast successes
  • Traffic: requests/sec for HTTP, data rate for databases, concurrent users for real-time
  • Errors: explicit errors (5xx), implicit errors (200 with wrong answer), degradation (slow responses)
  • Saturation: CPU, memory, disk I/O, network — also dependencies like connection pool exhaustion
  • Usage: create a "Four Golden Signals" dashboard per service — the first thing to check during an incident
  • Threshold: alert when any signal crosses a predefined threshold — correlate signals during root cause
lessons.why: The Golden Signals are the smallest set of metrics that give a comprehensive view of any service — a classic SRE interview topic.

lessons.name: Spans, Trace Context, and Trace Propagation
lessons.desc: A trace is a tree of spans. Each span represents a unit of work (an API call, a DB query). Spans carry: trace_id, span_id, parent_span_id, timestamps, attributes. Trace = entire request lifecycle across all services, Spa
lessons.what:
A trace is a tree of spans. Each span represents a unit of work (an API call, a DB query). Spans carry: trace_id, span_id, parent_span_id, timestamps, attributes.
  • Trace = entire request lifecycle across all services, Span = single operation within the trace
  • Trace_id identifies the entire trace — Span_id identifies the specific span
  • Parent_span_id creates the tree structure — root span has no parent
  • W3C Trace Context: traceparent header (version-trace_id-span_id-trace_flags)
  • Propagation: service extracts trace context from incoming request → creates child span → passes to downstream
  • Span attributes: service name, operation name, HTTP method, status code, duration, custom tags
lessons.why: Distributed tracing is the ONLY way to understand request flow across microservices — essential for debugging latency and failures.

lessons.name: Sampling Strategies — head-based, tail-based, probabilistic
lessons.desc: Sampling decides which traces to store. Head-based: sample at request entry. Tail-based: sample after seeing the full trace. Probabilistic: random percentage. Head-based sampling: decide at the root span — simple but mis
lessons.what:
Sampling decides which traces to store. Head-based: sample at request entry. Tail-based: sample after seeing the full trace. Probabilistic: random percentage.
  • Head-based sampling: decide at the root span — simple but misses errors that happen deep in the trace
  • Tail-based sampling: buffer all traces, decide at the end — captures all errors but requires more memory
  • Probabilistic sampling: random X% — unbiased but may miss rare events entirely
  • Smart sampling: always sample errors (anywhere in trace), sample slow traces, probabilistic for healthy ones
  • Rate limiting: max traces/second to avoid overwhelming the backend
  • OpenTelemetry Collector supports tail-based sampling via the tail_sampling processor
lessons.why: Storing every trace is prohibitively expensive — sampling strategy determines whether you capture important traces or miss critical data.

lessons.name: OpenTelemetry SDK & Collector — instrumentation, exporters, processors
lessons.desc: OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the vendor-neutral standard for instrumenting applications. SDK generates telemetry, Collector processes and exports to backends. OTel SDK: auto-instrumentation (zero-code via agent/hook) + manual
lessons.what:
OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the vendor-neutral standard for instrumenting applications. SDK generates telemetry, Collector processes and exports to backends.
  • OTel SDK: auto-instrumentation (zero-code via agent/hook) + manual instrumentation (via API)
  • OTel Collector: receivers (OTLP, Jaeger, Prometheus) → processors (batch, filter, sample) → exporters
  • OTLP protocol: binary, efficient, gRPC-based — the native protocol for OTel data exchange
  • Processors: batch (aggregate before export), attributes (add/remove tags), sampling (head/tail)
  • Exporters: send to any backend — Jaeger, Zipkin, Prometheus, Datadog, Grafana, self-hosted
  • OTel is CNCF graduated — it is the Linux Foundation of observability
lessons.why: OpenTelemetry is the industry standard — it replaces vendor-specific agents and gives you a unified instrumentation API.

lessons.name: Jaeger & Zipkin — trace storage, UI, and querying
lessons.desc: Jaeger (CNCF graduated, Go) and Zipkin (Finagle, Java) are the two dominant open-source tracing backends. They store traces and provide search/visualization UIs. Jaeger: Uber-born, Go, supports Elasticsearch/Cassandra/ba
lessons.what:
Jaeger (CNCF graduated, Go) and Zipkin (Finagle, Java) are the two dominant open-source tracing backends. They store traces and provide search/visualization UIs.
  • Jaeger: Uber-born, Go, supports Elasticsearch/Cassandra/badger storage, has deep dependency graph
  • Zipkin: Twitter-born, Java, supports Elasticsearch/Cassandra, simpler but less feature-rich
  • Jaeger UI: trace search by service/operation/tags, timeline view, flame graph, span details
  • Jaeger architecture: agent (sidecar) → collector → storage → query service → UI
  • Both support gRPC for trace ingestion and Web UI for trace exploration
  • OTel Collector can export to both: no need to choose between Jaeger and Zipkin
lessons.why: Tracing backends are your primary debugging tool for distributed latency — knowing how to navigate them is a core operations skill.

lessons.name: Trace-Log-Metric Correlation — linking telemetry signals
lessons.desc: The observability trifecta: logs reference trace_id, traces reference metric aggregations, metrics alert on anomaly that initiated the trace. All three linked for drill-down. Logs include trace_id and span_id in every st
lessons.what:
The observability trifecta: logs reference trace_id, traces reference metric aggregations, metrics alert on anomaly that initiated the trace. All three linked for drill-down.
  • Logs include trace_id and span_id in every structured log line — query "trace_id=abc" to see all logs
  • Metrics have label dimensions that map to service/operation — drill from metric to trace via exemplars
  • Exemplars: Prometheus feature that attaches a representative trace_id to a metric data point
  • Grafana Tempo: trace DB that integrates with Loki (logs) and Prometheus (metrics) for single-pane correlation
  • Workflow: Alert → metric graph → click exemplar → open trace → expand span → view associated logs
  • OpenTelemetry: logs emitted from within a span context automatically inherit trace_id and span_id
lessons.why: Correlation is the difference between having three tools and having ONE observability platform — it's what enables rapid root cause analysis.

lessons.name: Alerting Strategies — threshold, anomaly detection, predictive
lessons.desc: Threshold alerts fire when a metric crosses a boundary. Anomaly detection uses baselines. Predictive alerts forecast future issues. Each trades accuracy for complexity. Threshold: simple, hardcoded — "p99 latency > 500ms
lessons.what:
Threshold alerts fire when a metric crosses a boundary. Anomaly detection uses baselines. Predictive alerts forecast future issues. Each trades accuracy for complexity.
  • Threshold: simple, hardcoded — "p99 latency > 500ms for 5 minutes" — easy to understand, needs manual tuning
  • Anomaly detection: machine learning on historical data — detects subtle shifts, generates false positives early
  • Predictive: forecast-based — "predicted disk fill in 4 hours" — enables proactive remediation
  • Multi-condition: combine multiple signals — "high latency AND high CPU" reduces false alarms
  • Rate-of-change: "error rate increased 2x in 5 minutes" catches gradual degradation
  • Best practice: start with thresholds, add anomaly detection for hard-to-predict signals
lessons.why: Bad alerting causes incident fatigue (too many false positives) and blind spots (too few real alerts) — strategy determines which you get.

lessons.name: Alert Fatigue & Silencing — noise reduction, grouping, routing
lessons.desc: Alert fatigue occurs when teams receive too many irrelevant alerts. Solutions: grouping related alerts, silencing during maintenance, routing to the correct team. Grouping: Alertmanager groups similar alerts by labels (s
lessons.what:
Alert fatigue occurs when teams receive too many irrelevant alerts. Solutions: grouping related alerts, silencing during maintenance, routing to the correct team.
  • Grouping: Alertmanager groups similar alerts by labels (service, severity) into a single notification
  • Silencing: suppress alerts during deployments, maintenance windows, or known issues
  • Routing: route by severity (critical→PagerDuty, warning→Slack, info→dashboard)
  • Inhibition: higher-severity alert inhibits lower-severity alerts for the same service
  • Time-based: different routing on-call vs daytime — critical alerts always page, non-critical wait
  • Target: <5 alerts per on-call shift should require human action — everything else is noise
lessons.why: Alert fatigue is the #1 cause of missed critical incidents — if everything is urgent, nothing is urgent.

lessons.name: On-Call & Escalation — rotation, tiers, schedules
lessons.desc: On-call rotations distribute incident responsibility. Escalation policies define who gets paged when primary doesn't respond. Tiers route by severity. Rotation: weekly or bi-weekly shifts — avoid frequent rotation (disru
lessons.what:
On-call rotations distribute incident responsibility. Escalation policies define who gets paged when primary doesn't respond. Tiers route by severity.
  • Rotation: weekly or bi-weekly shifts — avoid frequent rotation (disrupts focus) and infrequent (rusty skills)
  • Follow-the-sun: rotate across timezone teams for 24h coverage without waking people at night
  • Tiers: L1 (initial triage), L2 (deep debugging), L3 (subject matter expert) — escalate up
  • Escalation: primary doesn't ack in N minutes → secondary → manager — auto-escalate, no manual intervention
  • Notification: PagerDuty/OpsGenie for critical (phone call), Slack for warning, email for info
  • Post-incident always: review if paging was appropriate — adjust rules based on false positives
lessons.why: Well-designed on-call processes prevent burnout and ensure incidents get the right attention — poorly designed ones lose engineers.

lessons.name: Incident Response & Runbooks — IR process, postmortems
lessons.desc: Incident response is a structured process: detect → triage → mitigate → resolve → postmortem. Runbooks provide step-by-step remediation procedures. IR phases: Detection → Triage (severity, assignee) → Mitigation (stop th
lessons.what:
Incident response is a structured process: detect → triage → mitigate → resolve → postmortem. Runbooks provide step-by-step remediation procedures.
  • IR phases: Detection → Triage (severity, assignee) → Mitigation (stop the bleeding) → Resolution (fix root cause) → Postmortem
  • Runbook: "What to do when [incident]" — includes dashboard links, debugging commands, rollback procedures
  • Blameless postmortem: focus on system/process failures, not individual mistakes — root cause = systemic cause
  • SLO tracking: was this incident within our error budget? Did we miss our SLO?
  • Action items: postmortem must produce concrete, tracked actions — "add alarm for X" not "monitor better"
  • Practice: game days and chaos engineering prepare teams for incidents before they happen in production
lessons.why: Without structured IR, incidents escalate chaotically — runbooks reduce MTTR by 50%+ and prevent repeated mistakes.

lessons.name: SLO-based Alerting — burn rate alerts, multi-window approach
lessons.desc: Burn rate alerts fire when error budget is consumed faster than expected. Multi-window approach: short window (fast detection) + long window (confirmation). Burn rate = error budget consumed / elapsed time — rate >1 mean
lessons.what:
Burn rate alerts fire when error budget is consumed faster than expected. Multi-window approach: short window (fast detection) + long window (confirmation).
  • Burn rate = error budget consumed / elapsed time — rate >1 means you will exhaust budget before window ends
  • Multi-window: 1m window (fast, noisy) + 5m window (slower, accurate) — fire if BOTH exceed threshold
  • Example: page if burn rate >15 over 5m AND >2 over 30m — catches fast burn with confirmation
  • SLO alerts are naturally contextual — they tell you "this matters to users" not just "metric spiked"
  • Implementation: Prometheus recording rules compute burn rate, Alertmanager routes by severity
  • Avoid static threshold alerts where SLO-based alerts apply — SLO alerts replace most threshold-based paging
lessons.why: SLO-based alerting is Google SRE's recommended approach — it alerts on business impact (are we burning budget?), not on symptom thresholds.

lessons.name: OpenTelemetry Ecosystem — CNCF landscape, OTLP, SDK maturity
lessons.desc: OpenTelemetry is the CNCF observability framework. It includes specification, SDKs in all major languages, Collector for processing/routing, and OTLP wire protocol. OTel specification: signals (traces/metrics/logs), cont
lessons.what:
OpenTelemetry is the CNCF observability framework. It includes specification, SDKs in all major languages, Collector for processing/routing, and OTLP wire protocol.
  • OTel specification: signals (traces/metrics/logs), context propagation, semantic conventions
  • SDKs: Go, Java, JS/TS, Python, .NET, Ruby, PHP, C++ — auto-instrumentation where available
  • OTel Collector: receiver (OTLP, Prometheus, Jaeger, Kafka) → processor → exporter (any backend)
  • OTLP protocol: protobuf over gRPC, supports compression, batching, and retries
  • Semantic conventions: standardized attribute names (http.method, db.system, cloud.provider)
  • OTel is CNCF graduated + W3C trace context — it's the Linux Foundation of observability
lessons.why: OTel is the de facto industry standard — vendor-neutral instrumentation means you're never locked into a proprietary agent.

lessons.name: Cost Optimization — storage tiering, sampling, retention strategies
lessons.desc: Observability costs scale linearly with data volume. Optimization: sample aggressively, tier storage, reduce cardinality, set retention policies per signal type. Metrics: reduce cardinality — limit unique label combinati
lessons.what:
Observability costs scale linearly with data volume. Optimization: sample aggressively, tier storage, reduce cardinality, set retention policies per signal type.
  • Metrics: reduce cardinality — limit unique label combinations, aggregate dimensions where possible
  • Traces: head-based sampling (cheapest) vs tail-based (better quality but 3-5x cost)
  • Logs: hot (7 days), warm (30 days, compressed), cold (1 year+, object storage) — delete what has no value
  • Storage engines: object storage (S3/GCS) for cold data is 10-100x cheaper than SSD-based storage
  • Cost allocation: tag telemetry by team/service/environment — chargeback drives responsible usage
  • Rule of thumb: 1:10:100 ratio for hot:warm:cold storage costs per GB/month
lessons.why: Observability bills (Datadog, Grafana Cloud) can exceed infrastructure costs — optimization is a necessary architect skill.

lessons.name: Platform Observability — internal developer platform, self-service
lessons.desc: Platform observability treats observability as a product. Platform team provides self-service dashboards, pre-configured alerts, and instrumentation libraries. Platform: standardized OTel SDK configuration, pre-built das
lessons.what:
Platform observability treats observability as a product. Platform team provides self-service dashboards, pre-configured alerts, and instrumentation libraries.
  • Platform: standardized OTel SDK configuration, pre-built dashboards per service archetype
  • Service archetypes: HTTP API (RED), queue consumer (lag, throughput), cron (success, duration)
  • Dashboards: generated from service metadata — deploy manifest declares SLO, dashboard auto-creates
  • Alert templates: pre-defined alert strategies per archetype — devs just set SLO targets
  • Doc: runbook template, on-call playbook, incident response checklist — embedded in service repo
  • Maturity: Level 2 (instrumentation) is reactive — Level 3 (platform) is proactive and scalable
lessons.why: Self-service observability scales engineering without growing the platform team — developers instrument their own services correctly.

lessons.name: Observability-Driven Development — cultural adoption & DevEx
lessons.desc: Observability-driven development means instrumenting as you code, not after deployment. Treat telemetry as a first-class product requirement. Shift-left observability: add OTel spans and structured logs during feature de
lessons.what:
Observability-driven development means instrumenting as you code, not after deployment. Treat telemetry as a first-class product requirement.
  • Shift-left observability: add OTel spans and structured logs during feature development, not after
  • DevEx: instant feedback via local telemetry export — developers see traces in dev environment
  • Contract testing: verify that telemetry is emitted correctly in CI — failing = failed PR
  • Culture: blameless postmortems encourage honest instrumentation — fear of blame hides data
  • Standards: service must emit health check, RED metrics, structured logs, critical-path traces
  • Mantra: "if you can't observe it, you can't operate it" — observability is a non-functional requirement
lessons.why: Retrofitting observability is 10x more expensive than building it in — making it part of dev workflow is the only scalable approach.

lessons.name: CPU Profiling — flame graphs, sampling profilers, continuous profiling
lessons.desc: CPU profiling captures which functions consume CPU time. Flame graphs visualize call stacks (width = CPU time). Sampling profilers (async-profiler, pprof) capture stacks at intervals with low overhead. Flame graph: x-axi
lessons.what:
CPU profiling captures which functions consume CPU time. Flame graphs visualize call stacks (width = CPU time). Sampling profilers (async-profiler, pprof) capture stacks at intervals with low overhead.
  • Flame graph: x-axis = stack depth, y-axis = CPU percentage — wide bars = hot functions
  • Sampling profilers: interrupt every 10ms, record call stack — ~1-3% overhead in production
  • Continuous profiling: always-on profiling in production (Pyroscope, Datadog Profiling, Parca)
  • Go: go tool pprof (heap, cpu, goroutine, mutex), net/http/pprof endpoint
  • Java: async-profiler (uses perf_events, no safepoint bias), JFR (Java Flight Recorder)
  • Production: continuous profiling with 1-minute resolution catches regressions before they hit SLO
lessons.why: Profiling answers "where is CPU time actually spent?" — it's the only way to find real performance bottlenecks vs imagined ones.

lessons.name: Memory Profiling — heap dumps, leak detection, allocation tracking
lessons.desc: Memory profiling tracks heap allocations and identifies leaks. Heap snapshots compare two points in time to find growing objects. Allocation tracking shows where memory is created. Heap snapshot: capture all live objects
lessons.what:
Memory profiling tracks heap allocations and identifies leaks. Heap snapshots compare two points in time to find growing objects. Allocation tracking shows where memory is created.
  • Heap snapshot: capture all live objects at a point in time — compare two snapshots to find growth
  • Chrome DevTools: Heap Snapshots, Allocation Timeline, Allocation Profiler
  • Node.js: --inspect flag + Chrome DevTools, or heapdump module for programmatic snapshots
  • Java: jmap -dump:live, MAT (Memory Analyzer Tool) for leak detection
  • Go: pprof heap profile, go tool pprof -http=:8080 for web UI
  • Sign: steady memory growth without corresponding load increase = likely leak
lessons.why: Memory leaks in production cause OOM crashes — heap profiling is the only reliable way to find root cause.

lessons.name: eBPF Fundamentals — kernel instrumentation without kernel changes
lessons.desc: eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) runs sandboxed programs in the kernel without modifying kernel source. It hooks into syscalls, network events, and kernel functions for deep observability. eBPF programs run in kern
lessons.what:
eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) runs sandboxed programs in the kernel without modifying kernel source. It hooks into syscalls, network events, and kernel functions for deep observability.
  • eBPF programs run in kernel space in a safe sandbox (verifier ensures no crashes)
  • Hook points: syscalls, kprobes, tracepoints, network events (XDP, TC)
  • Use cases: network monitoring (Cilium), security (Falco), tracing (bpftrace), profiling (Pixie)
  • bpftrace: one-liner tracing language — bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_* { @[comm] = count(); }'
  • Cilium: CNI for Kubernetes using eBPF for networking, service mesh, and network policy
  • Overhead: <1% CPU for most eBPF programs — far lower than traditional agents
lessons.why: eBPF provides kernel-level observability with near-zero overhead — it's the most powerful observability technology of the decade.

lessons.name: Production Profiling Workflow — how to use profiles to optimize performance
lessons.desc: Profile in production (continuous profiling) → find top CPU consumers → correlate with request traces → optimize → verify improvement → deploy. Step 1: Enable continuous profiling (Pyroscope, Parca, or cloud-native like
lessons.what:
Profile in production (continuous profiling) → find top CPU consumers → correlate with request traces → optimize → verify improvement → deploy.
  • Step 1: Enable continuous profiling (Pyroscope, Parca, or cloud-native like Datadog)
  • Step 2: Find top CPU/memory consumers by service, endpoint, or code path
  • Step 3: Correlate with traces — which slow request was caused by this function?
  • Step 4: Optimize (algorithm, caching, reduce allocations, parallelize) — measure before/after
  • Step 5: Deploy with profiling enabled — verify improvement in production metrics
  • Anti-pattern: optimizing code that isn't a bottleneck — profile first, optimize second
lessons.why: Most performance optimization without profiling is guesswork — profiling provides evidence-based optimization.

lessons.name: Frontend Observability — RUM, Core Web Vitals, error tracking
lessons.desc: Frontend observability captures user experience data. Real User Monitoring (RUM) tracks actual user sessions. Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) measure performance. Frontend error tracking (Sentry, LogRocket) captures JS e
lessons.what:
Frontend observability captures user experience data. Real User Monitoring (RUM) tracks actual user sessions. Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) measure performance. Frontend error tracking (Sentry, LogRocket) captures JS errors with session replay.
  • Real User Monitoring (RUM): captures page load, interaction timing, errors from actual users
  • Core Web Vitals: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint <2.5s), INP (Interaction to Next Paint <200ms), CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift <0.1)
  • Frontend errors: unhandled Promise rejections, rendering errors, network failures — caught by window.onerror, window.onunhandledrejection
  • Session replay: replay user sessions to debug issues (LogRocket, FullStory, Sentry Session Replay)
  • Correlation: trace frontend spans to backend traces via traceparent header (W3C)
  • Tools: Sentry (error tracking), Datadog RUM, New Relic Browser, OpenTelemetry JS SDK
lessons.why: Backend metrics can show 200 OK while users experience broken UIs — frontend observability closes the observability gap.

lessons.name: Synthetic Monitoring — uptime checks, scripted journeys, canary testing
lessons.desc: Synthetic monitoring runs automated tests from external locations to simulate user behavior. Uptime checks verify availability. Scripted journeys test critical paths (login, checkout). Canaries deploy to small % and veri
lessons.what:
Synthetic monitoring runs automated tests from external locations to simulate user behavior. Uptime checks verify availability. Scripted journeys test critical paths (login, checkout). Canaries deploy to small % and verify health.
  • Uptime monitoring: HTTP checks from multiple regions, verify status code, response time, SSL certificate expiry
  • Synthetic scripts: Playwright/Puppeteer scripts that simulate user journeys (login → browse → checkout)
  • API monitoring: periodic API calls to verify response schema, latency SLAs, error rates
  • Canary deployments: deploy to 5% traffic, verify error rates stay below threshold, auto-rollback if breach
  • Tools: Pingdom (uptime), Checkly (synthetic scripts), Datadog Synthetics, Grafana k6
  • Limitation: synthetic ≠ real — doesn't capture real user performance, device diversity, or network conditions
lessons.why: Synthetic monitoring catches issues before real users are affected — it proactively validates user-facing functionality.

lessons.name: APM as a Concept — Application Performance Monitoring, distributed tracing integration
lessons.desc: APM is the practice of monitoring application performance end-to-end. It combines metrics (latency, throughput, error rate), traces (request flow), and logs into a unified view. APM agents auto-instrument code and collec
lessons.what:
APM is the practice of monitoring application performance end-to-end. It combines metrics (latency, throughput, error rate), traces (request flow), and logs into a unified view. APM agents auto-instrument code and collect telemetry.
  • APM pillars: metrics (RED/USE), distributed traces, logs, errors, and real user data
  • Auto-instrumentation: APM agents inject tracing/logging without code changes (Datadog agent, New Relic agent)
  • Service maps: auto-generated dependency graphs from trace data — shows which services talk to each other
  • Transaction tracing: capture a single request across all services, show time spent in each
  • Baselines: APM tools learn normal behavior and alert on anomalies (not static thresholds)
  • APM vs observability: APM is a tool category, observability is a property — APM helps achieve observability
lessons.why: APM provides the big picture — from user click to database query — making it the primary tool for performance diagnosis.
